Overview

Azure Security Center reports a campaign, seen in April 2020 across tens of Kubernetes clusters, that targeted Kubeflow, the machine-learning toolkit for Kubernetes, to run cryptocurrency miners: ML nodes are powerful and often have GPUs. The same image from a public repository, which runs an XMRIG miner, appeared on many clusters, and most of those clusters ran Kubeflow, which pointed to the ML framework as the way in. The post explains the weakness. Kubeflow's dashboard sits behind an Istio ingress gateway that is internal by default, but some users switch that service to a load balancer for convenience, which puts the dashboard on the Internet and lets anyone perform operations in Kubeflow. Whoever reaches it can deploy containers, either by starting a Jupyter notebook server with a custom image or by running code in a notebook whose mounted service account may deploy containers in its namespace. The campaign is mapped onto Microsoft's threat matrix for Kubernetes, and the post closes with detection commands and controls: authentication, monitoring public endpoints, restricting public load balancers and allowing only trusted images.

Limits

  • Thin numbers. Tens of clusters, observed during April; no counts, victims or dates beyond that.
  • The access vector is inferred. It rests on most affected clusters running Kubeflow and on the default namespace name "anonymous" appearing widely, not on a reconstructed intrusion.
  • A product post. It ends by inviting readers to try Azure Security Center.
  • 2020 defaults. The behaviour described is Kubeflow's as of 2020; current defaults were not checked here.
  • A live page. The digest covers today's HTML, which wraps the 2020 text in current site navigation, so it will not match a capture from another day.
